prose: Daily pH titration of the bunker mother culture registered a steady pH 3.85. The symbiotic 100:1 population ratio of *Lactobacillus sanfranciscensis* to *Candida humilis* wild yeast produced a balanced 3.2:1 lactic-to-acetic acid profile, giving bread its characteristic tangy aroma.

Executing a strict 12-hour feeding cycle with equal parts stone-ground whole rye flour and de-chlorinated well water (100% hydration) doubled starter volume within four hours. Robust carbon dioxide bubbles lifted the dense stoneware lid.

Oxygen exposure inside a loosely sealed crock allowed aerobic *Pichia membranifaciens* (kahm yeast) to establish a wrinkled white film across the starter. Scraping the surface pellicle and acidifying with pure mother starter salvaged the underlying yeast core.

Allowing fermentation temperatures to linger at 32°C drove pH down to 3.45. Extreme acidity activated flour aspartic proteinases, which digested the gluten network and liquefied fifty kilograms of bread dough into a sticky, un-kneadable puddle.

During winter grain rationing, bakers placed mother culture jars into the 4°C potato cellar. After forty-five days of dormant chilling without feeding, a single warm refreshment restored active bubbling within eight hours.

Starved yeast cells exhausted available maltose sugars and entered stationary phase, secreting a dark, aromatic 8% ABV ethanolic liquid layer ('hooch'). Decanting the hooch and dosing with fresh wheat middlings quickly restored cellular vigor.

A virulent lytic bacteriophage epidemic destroyed the dominant *Lactobacillus* colony inside Bakery Bay 1. Without bacterial lactic acid production, culture pH stalled at 5.10, allowing putrefactive bacteria to produce foul, sulfurous off-odors.

Spreading ripe sourdough starter into paper-thin sheets across linen cloth and air-drying with sterile 22°C dehumidified air yielded brittle dried flakes. Sealed inside airtight glass vials with desiccant, the flakes remained 100% viable for over a decade.
